subject: clockworkDog
pitch: A wind-up clockwork terrier made of polished brass and copper. Riveted body plates, visible gears turning in its chest, a big winding key on its back, springy jointed legs, floppy leather ears, glass-lens eyes with a green tint, a tail made of a coiled spring, and a little red collar with a brass tag.
reasoning:
I'm planning out a terrier model as a TypeScript module, working out realistic proportions and a skeleton structure starting from the hips and spine chain forward to the neck.

Still designing joint hierarchy...

So for legs with four points—hip, knee, ankle, and paw—I'll need four names total, with a "leg" role on the chain and manual polyline coordinates rather than an IK-based limb helper. For the tail, I'm thinking of a chain going back and up from the hips, possibly with a coiled spring effect made from a spiral sweep in a copper color attached near the tip.

Working out the spiral coil geometry...

Now I'm settling on a color palette — brass, copper, dark leather tones, red, and a green tint for the lens — and starting to lay out the riveted body plates using basic box geometry.

For the torso, I'm sweeping a tube along the spine chain with a radius that gently oscillates for a segmented, bony look, keyed to the chain's bones directly. For the chest, I'm planning visible gears using cylinder geometry with teeth-like segments to suggest turning mechanisms.

I'm working out the chest gear placement, positioning copper discs on the body's outer surface facing forward, and figuring out the right z-coordinate so they sit flush against the bulge of the torso sweep rather than floating off the surface.

Placing a brass chest plate near the top of the spine around z=0.29, then adding copper gear discs mounted on its front face facing outward along z.

For the head, I'm keeping things manageable by using a simple elongated box attached to a head bone positioned forward from the neck, with a separate jaw joint parented to the head to support an upper and lower mouth structure, plus a snout box extended forward and eye lenses to follow.

Now for the ears, I'm planning a flat extruded teardrop shape hanging on the sides of the head, oriented in the y-z plane with thickness along x to give it a floppy leather look.

I'll keep the ears angled slightly for a floppy look, colored dark brown leather. Now moving to the legs, I need four polyline chains with hip joints for the rear legs and shoulders for the front, setting the spine height and depth to anchor the body frame.

For each leg, I'm defining four points—hip/shoulder, knee, ankle, and paw—with the paw resting near y=0 so the feet touch the ground, giving each a joint chain of named points plus a tip. I'll sweep these with a thin brass-colored radius to get a springy, wiry leg look.

Rather than building separate sweep calls per leg, I realize the chain itself can sweep its own bones directly, with front legs parenting to a higher spine joint and rear legs to a lower one so the body connects naturally. For the feet, I'm considering adding small spheres at each leg's tip joint, using the chain's tip reference directly as the position so the foot sits exactly at the paw point.

For the tail, I'm setting up a short catmull-rom chain off the hips parented to the first spine joint, then continuing it into a coiled spring using a spiral sweep whose center and axis extend from the tail tip in the direction the tail curves upward and back.

I decide to anchor the coil directly at the tail tip so the spring reads as a continuation of the tail rather than floating separately, tapering its radius from base to end across several turns with a copper-colored sweep. Next I'll add a torus for the key on the back, oriented upright.

Placing the key ring and its shaft, I need to recalc the mounting height against the spine's catmull points — the body top sits around y 0.56 where z=0, so the key base should start there, and I'm rechecking leg length proportions against the body's bottom edge to keep the silhouette balanced.

Now I'm shifting focus to the head rig: a neck chain running from the spine's last point up to a forward head joint, then building the skull via a sphere, a snout box, a dark nose sphere, and starting the jaw joint positioning relative to the head.

Next I'm defining the jaw joint's aim direction and attaching a lower jaw box bone, then setting up the ears to follow the head bone using local coordinates. For the eyes, I'm placing glass spheres with brass torus rings around them, oriented to face forward along the head's direction.

Now I'm working out a collar — a red torus ring positioned around the neck geometry, calculating the midpoint between neck joints to center it, with the ring dimensions sized to fit snugly around the neck's radius.

I'm then approximating the position for a small brass tag hanging below it, trying to estimate where the neck's axis passes through to place the tag near the front-bottom of the collar.

For the chest gears, I'm reconsidering placement—rather than the actual front of the torso, I think putting visible gear plates on the side flanks makes more sense, with gear disks facing outward near the mid-body so they read as "gears turning in its chest" while staying structurally sound.

Still writing gear geometry...

Realizing chain.at gives the centerline, not the surface, so I need rivets placed on the actual body plate surface instead -- thinking through using a surface scatter or stick method to get hit points along the torso sweep for rivet placement.

The spine chain's parametric sweep handles both the torso shape and rivet placement using the same t value from the source chain, which keeps things consistent. Now I'm setting up the hip joint position and working out leg placement, defining hip, knee, and ankle points for the rear legs with the knee angled backward.

For front legs I'm placing hip, knee, ankle, and paw joints with a slight forward tilt so the paws make clean ground contact, using small sweep radii that taper to meet the floor at y=0. I'm naming each of the four leg chains using side (L/R) and front/rear identifiers like shoulderFL, elbowFL, wristFL, and pawFL to keep bone names unique and valid.

For the "springy" legs look, I'm considering adding a small copper spiral wrapped around the lower leg segment, computed as a spiral sweep centered on the knee-to-ankle midpoint with vertical axis, several turns, and a small pitch and radius to approximate a coiled spring without overcomplicating the model.

Still positioning spring coils...

I'll keep the body paint flat and use glass eye coloring, naming the root joint "hips" and wrapping everything in a builder module with a clean export structure. I need to be careful only importing what's actually used from the builder library to avoid unused-import issues, then move on to extruding the ear geometry near the head's upper-back region with leather coloring and a slight bevel.

For the ear itself, I'm positioning it hanging down from the side of the skull with a simple drop rather than adding complicated tilt directions—attaching near the top and letting it fall down about 0.14 units with modest thickness. I'll skip teeth details on the jaw for now and just set up the mouth as upper and lower boxes, then move on to finalizing colors.

Now I'm picking the material palette—brass, copper, red, leather, glass, dark, and a brighter rivet brass—and treating the eyes as glass domes ringed in brass. For the tail, I'm chaining it off the hips joint with a curved catmull path rising and sweeping back, capping it with a small coiled spring effect using a normalized axis, and considering making the whole tail itself a coiled spring rather than a plain tapered chain.

Working out the tail's spring geometry: computing the axis direction between the base and tip points, then building a spiral with several turns and a set pitch so its length matches the tail's extension, while also adding a thin core rod underneath for structure so the coil wraps around something solid.

I'm setting up the tail as a chain with a few catmull points, then wrapping a spiral spring tube around it with copper coloring, and now starting to write the actual TypeScript code importing the builder utilities.

I'm defining the color palette (brass, rivet, copper, leather, glass tones) and starting the skeleton build, setting the hips joint as root and building the spine as a catmull chain parented to it, making sure there's exactly one root joint without a parent before moving on to define the neck.

Continuing the chain, I'm setting up the neck as a catmull chain parented to the spine, then placing the head joint at the neck's end with an aim direction, followed by a jaw joint parented to the head using local offsets for position and aim. Now I'm starting the head geometry, sketching out a blocky skull shape using box or sphere primitives in the brass material.

Still placing head parts...

Defining the ear outline shape and positioning, then working out the chest gear placements with a radius function that bulges mid-torso and tapers toward the neck, plus brass plates mounted behind the gears on each flank.

Now I'm simplifying the gear design into a torus bezel with a copper disc hub, adding a second smaller meshing gear per side, and writing a helper function to generate the hub and teeth geometry for each gear.

Still writing gear function...

After that I'll plan rivets along the torso sweep, placing them at specific sweep positions and angular offsets, with the gears sitting roughly on the flanks near ±90 degrees around the tube.

Still placing plates...

Realizing the fixed plate position would get buried by the spine's varying radius, I'm reconsidering the approach—maybe skip discrete plates and instead sweep the body with a banded color pattern to simulate riveted copper panels, or alternatively build the body from separate panel sweeps following the spine curve.

Adding rivet placement logic...

I'm also checking where the gear flanks land relative to chest sectors, confirming the rivets at different t and angle values don't overlap badly. Then I'm figuring out where the back key sits on the spine, computing spine height at that z position so the key base aligns with the top copper panel correctly.

Now I'm working out the key ring and shaft placement — centering the torus ring above the shaft top so it doesn't clip, orienting its sweep plane correctly, then moving to the neck collar, picking a torus radius slightly larger than the neck sweep radius and aligning its direction along the neck's curve so it sits naturally at the joint.

Next I'm computing where a hanging tag would attach to the collar's underside-front, using perpendicular vectors to find that point, then sizing a small brass disc as a thin cylinder to represent the tag.

I'm now plotting the leg joint positions for both front and rear legs, setting hip, knee, ankle, and paw coordinates to create a believable digitigrade stance, then starting to write the loop that builds named joint chains for the left and right legs.

Working out spring coil placement at the ankles, picking center points, axes, and spiral parameters so the copper spring sits proportionally against the leg sweep radius.

Now I'm figuring out the paw geometry, deciding to pass the leg's last joint explicitly as the bone reference for proper attachment, then starting on the tail chain with a catmull spline and matching joint names before sweeping it with a thin radius.

For the coiled tail segment, I'm checking that the spiral geometry's axis direction matches the tail's actual direction vector, and confirming tube radius versus coil radius proportions look right. I'm then placing a copper winding key cylinder near the tail, debating whether to anchor it to a specific spine joint rather than relying on the nearest-joint default for more rigid attachment.

Working through the key ring torus placement and rotation, confirming rivet and head-plate attachments look fine, and verifying that the gear-building closure correctly uses the builder's part method. I'm making sure the module exports a meta object with name and description, then double-checking each builder call signature—joint, chain with a catmull path—for correctness.

Still checking API signatures...

I'll just inline the ear outline literal directly in both mirrored calls to avoid typing issues, confirming torus parameter order and joint typing are fine. Now I'm working through the jaw joint setup, head-relative positioning, and the eye/pupil geometry placement using local coordinate frames.

Next I'm sketching out a gear helper taking center, normal, radius, and teeth count, then placing a big and small gear on the chest flank so their edges roughly mesh, plus considering a brass bezel plate behind them as a window frame.

Now I'm adding rivet rows along the torso using a stick helper that places small spheres at parameterized points and angles, looping over both flank sides and a few positions along the body, with extra rows for the plate seams near the gears.
